text: Sometimes a column name collides with a reserved word, or has a space in it, and you need a way to quote it so the parser knows it's a name, not a keyword. Every platform solves this, but each one reaches for a different character. Let's go through SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.

In T-SQL, square brackets are the classic answer — bracket Order, bracket Customer Name. Brackets always work, with no configuration needed. SQL Server will also accept standard double quotes, but only when the QUOTED_IDENTIFIER session setting is on — which is the default in most tools, but not guaranteed in every script or driver, so brackets are the safer bet.

Oracle and PostgreSQL both skip brackets entirely and use the ANSI-standard double quote — quote Order quote, quote Customer Name quote — identical syntax on both. The wrinkle, which we'll dig into fully next lesson, is that quoting an identifier also makes it case-sensitive on both of these platforms.

MySQL's default is the backtick — backtick Order backtick, backtick Customer Name backtick. MySQL can technically be switched to accept double quotes instead, by turning on the ANSI_QUOTES SQL mode, but that's rarely flipped on in practice. In the real world, backticks are what you'll see in MySQL code.

So to recap: brackets on SQL Server, double quotes on Oracle and PostgreSQL, backticks on MySQL — three different default characters across four platforms, and MySQL is the one exception that can be reconfigured. Next lesson: what happens to case sensitivity once you start quoting those names.
